config.title: Build tabs with keyboard navigation

intro.title: Build tabs with keyboard navigation
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build an accessible tabbed interface that users can navigate using their keyboard. You will learn how to manage component state to track the active tab and handle user interactions. The core programming concepts involve using React hooks like useState for state management and useEffect for side effects, along with event handlers for keyboard inputs. You'll work with JSX to structure the tab buttons and content panels, ensuring proper ARIA attributes for accessibility. By the end, you'll have a functional tab component that responds to arrow keys and the Enter or Space key for activation.
intro.usecase: Tabbed interfaces with keyboard navigation are essential for accessibility and productivity in modern web applications. You'll find them in content-heavy dashboards like analytics platforms (Google Analytics, Mixpanel) where users switch between different data views, or in admin panels where sections like Users, Settings, and Reports are organized in tabs. Developers implement this pattern in documentation sites with code examples, e-commerce product detail pages with Description/Reviews/Specs tabs, and any multi-panel UI where keyboard users need efficient navigation without reaching for their mouse.

objectives: Construct a tabbed interface with clickable tab buttons and corresponding content panels.
Initialize and manage the active tab state using JavaScript.
Implement keyboard event handlers to navigate between tabs using arrow keys.
Control focus management to ensure keyboard users can interact with the active tab content.
Update the UI dynamically to reflect the currently selected tab and its content.
Integrate ARIA attributes to enhance accessibility for screen reader users.
Manipulate DOM elements to show and hide tab panels based on user interaction.

steps.title: Import React and useState
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in the necessary modules for building React components and managing state.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing modules for a different component
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: The React library and useState hook are imported and available for use in the component.
successCriteria: React and useState are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure to import both React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The import statement is missing or incorrect. Please import React and useState from 'react'.

steps.title: Create the Tabs component
steps.instruction: Define a function component named Tabs that returns null for now.
steps.hint: Create a function called Tabs that returns null. You can use either a function declaration or an arrow function.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Define the Tabs component here
steps.expectedOutcome: A Tabs component is defined and returns null.
successCriteria: The Tabs component is defined as a function and returns null.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the Tabs component structure.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure the component is named Tabs and returns null.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component isn't defined correctly. Create a function named Tabs that returns null.

steps.title: Initialize active tab state
steps.instruction: Inside your Tabs component, use the useState hook to create a state variable called activeTab initialized to 0.
steps.hint: Call useState with the initial value 0 and destructure the returned array into activeTab and a setter function.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: initializing state
const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have an activeTab state variable tracking which tab is currently active, starting with the first tab (index 0).
successCriteria: The Tabs component contains a useState call that declares activeTab state initialized to 0.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using useState to create a state variable named activeTab initialized to 0 inside the Tabs component.
steps.feedbackWrong: The activeTab state isn't properly initialized. Remember to use useState(0) inside your Tabs component and destructure the array into [activeTab, setActiveTab].

steps.title: Define tab data array
steps.instruction: Inside your Tabs component, create a constant array named 'tabsData' containing objects for three tabs. Each object should have 'id', 'label', and 'content' properties.
steps.hint: Define the array with const tabsData = [ ... ] and include three objects inside the array brackets. Use meaningful labels and content text for each tab.
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a tabsData array with three tab objects, each containing id, label, and content properties.
successCriteria: The tabsData array is defined with three objects, each containing id, label, and content properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure tabsData is an array with exactly three objects, each containing id, label, and content properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: Create a constant array named 'tabsData' with three objects inside, each having id, label, and content properties.

steps.title: Create handleTabClick handler
steps.instruction: Inside your Tabs component, define a function called handleTabClick that takes an index parameter and updates the activeTab state with that index.
steps.hint: Create a function that calls setActiveTab with the provided index.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a handleTabClick function that can update the active tab state when called with an index.
successCriteria: The handleTabClick function is defined, takes an index parameter, and calls setActiveTab with that index.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your function takes an index parameter and calls setActiveTab with it.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function isn't defined correctly. It should take an index and update the activeTab state.

steps.title: Create handleKeyDown handler
steps.instruction: Define a function called handleKeyDown inside your Tabs component. This function should take an event parameter and handle keyboard navigation for the tabs.
steps.hint: Start by writing: const handleKeyDown = (event) => { ... } or function handleKeyDown(event) { ... } inside your component, after the handleTabClick function.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a handleKeyDown function defined in your component, ready to implement keyboard navigation logic in the next step.
successCriteria: A handleKeyDown function is defined inside the Tabs component, taking an event parameter.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've defined a function named handleKeyDown that accepts an event parameter inside your Tabs component.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleKeyDown function isn't properly defined. Check that you've created a function with the correct name and parameter inside your component.

steps.title: Return the main container
steps.instruction: In your Tabs component, return a div element with the className 'tabs' as the main container.
steps.hint: The return statement should output a JSX div with the specified class name.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now returns a main container div with the class 'tabs', ready to hold the tab structure.
successCriteria: The Tabs component returns a div with className 'tabs'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the return statement outputs a div with exactly className='tabs'.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you're returning a div element with the correct className attribute.

steps.title: Create tab buttons container
steps.instruction: Inside the main container div, add a new div element with role='tablist' and className='tab-list' to serve as the container for your tab buttons.
steps.hint: Add a <div> with the specified role and className attributes inside the existing <div className="tabs">.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should see a tablist container div with proper accessibility role and styling class added inside your main tabs container.
successCriteria: A div element with role='tablist' and className='tab-list' is added inside the main container.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a container, but make sure it has both role='tablist' and className='tab-list' attributes.
steps.feedbackWrong: The tablist container wasn't added correctly. You need to add a div element with role='tablist' and className='tab-list' inside the main container.

steps.title: Render tab buttons with click handler
steps.instruction: Inside the tablist container, map through the tabsData array to create a button for each tab. For each button, set its key to the index, its text content to the tab's label, and wire its onClick handler to call handleTabClick with the index.
steps.hint: Use the map method on tabsData. For each item, return a button element with the required attributes.
steps.expectedOutcome: The tablist container will contain three buttons labeled 'Tab 1', 'Tab 2', and 'Tab 3', each with a click handler that updates the active tab state.
successCriteria: The tabsData array is mapped to create button elements, each with a unique key, the correct label text, and an onClick handler that calls handleTabClick with the corresponding index.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started mapping the tabs, but check that each button has a key, displays the correct label, and calls handleTabClick with the index.
steps.feedbackWrong: The tab buttons aren't rendering correctly. Make sure to map through tabsData and return a button for each item with the required attributes.

steps.title: Add keyboard navigation to tab buttons
steps.instruction: Add an onKeyDown event handler to each tab button in the map function that calls the handleKeyDown function.
steps.hint: Inside the button element you're mapping, add onKeyDown={handleKeyDown} after the onClick handler.
steps.analogousExample:
// Adding keyboard event handler to a button
<button onClick={handleClick} onKeyDown={handleKeyDown}>
  Click me
</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: Each tab button will have both click and keyboard event handlers attached.
successCriteria: All tab buttons have an onKeyDown attribute that calls handleKeyDown.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure each button has onKeyDown={handleKeyDown}.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try adding onKeyDown={handleKeyDown} to each button element inside the map function.

steps.title: Create tab content area
steps.instruction: After the tablist div, add a div element with role='tabpanel' and className='tab-content' to display the active tab's content.
steps.hint: Place the new div right after the closing of the tablist. Use the activeTab index to get the content from tabsData.
steps.expectedOutcome: A new div with role='tabpanel' and className='tab-content' appears after the tablist, ready to display content.
successCriteria: A div with role='tabpanel' and className='tab-content' is added after the tablist div.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added a div, but check that it has both role='tabpanel' and className='tab-content' attributes.
steps.feedbackWrong: The tab content area is missing. Add a div with role='tabpanel' and className='tab-content' after the tablist.

steps.title: Display active tab content
steps.instruction: Inside the tab content area, display the content from tabsData based on the activeTab state.
steps.hint: Access the content property of the tab object at the activeTab index in tabsData.
steps.analogousExample:
// Display content from an array based on state
const content = items[activeIndex].content;
steps.expectedOutcome: The tab content area shows the content of the currently active tab.
successCriteria: The tab content area displays the content from tabsData[activeTab].content.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! The active tab's content is now displayed.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're accessing the content property from the correct tab in tabsData.
steps.feedbackWrong: The content area isn't showing the active tab's content. Check that you're using tabsData[activeTab].content inside the tab-content div.
